newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan govt should not intervene in currencies - MOF.
newsitem.headline: Japan govt should not intervene in currencies - MOF.

text.p: The Japanese government should not intervene in the currency market, newly appointed Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told Reuters on Friday.
Foreign exchange markets move in line with trends in global trade and the world's market economy, he said.
"Markets are by nature things that move, and all I can say is that we will keep careful watch. It's not something that we should intervene in," Mitsuzuka said, without elaborating.
"The market will naturally reflect the strength of Japan's economy, and I am not very worried (about the current state of the foreign exchange market)," he said.
"The market is moving in a way that reflects (Japan's) overall economic conditions," Mitsuzuka said.
In order to put the economy on a stable growth trend, it is important to steadily implement fiscal and monetary policies such as fiscal reforms and flexibility in formulating a state budget, he said.
Mitsuzuka said there was no doubt that Japan's economy was on a gradual recovery trend, but not all industries were on a recovery trend as was shown in various surveys.

Regarding the fact that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) has kept the official discount rate at a record low of 0.5 percent for more than a year, he said the primary and secondary industries as well as small firms were happy with this situation.
Asked whether the BOJ was likely to maintain the current policy of keeping interest rates low, Mitsuzuka said: "Yes, I think this will continue."
Asked whether such a policy was needed to help the economy, he said: "I think we do need it, at the moment."

Regarding a supplementary budget for fiscal 1996/97 ending March, he said the government would draft a budget to cover the necessary costs for areas such as those for the reconstruction of Kobe after the earthquake there in January 1995, and for funds to help the growth of new technologies centreing on information and communications.
However, the government cannot follow the precedent of heaping money on public works, Mitsuzuka said when asked whether stimulative measures should be included in the extra budget.

Regarding the revision of laws to boost the central bank's independence, Mitsuzuka said he would like to see the government submit bills to the next regular session of parliament starting in January and make them into law.
He said he would respect a report to be submitted by a governmental study group on the issue, and make any additions to it if needed, as the issue also concerns his ministry.
The study group is expected to submit the report to the prime minister by the end of this year.
